title: DBMS Foundations
subtitle: Architecture, data independence, keys and integrity constraints — exam-oriented practice.
source: DBMS Crash Course Part 1 — Modules 1 to 4. Questions are independently crafted from the module concepts and exam-style patterns supplied for Bank SO IT.
instructions: Choose one answer for each question.
Questions are designed for IBPS SO IT, RRB Scale II IT, SBI SO and similar Computer Science/IT examinations.
Review the explanation, important point, exam trap and hint after submission.

questions.question: Which statement most accurately distinguishes a database from a DBMS?

options.text: A database is the software that manages data, whereas a DBMS is the stored data.
A database is an organized collection of related data, whereas a DBMS is software used to manage it.
A database is always a set of tables, whereas a DBMS is only a query language.
A database and a DBMS are two names for exactly the same thing.

questions.explanation: A database refers to the organized collection of related data; the DBMS provides the software facilities to create, store, retrieve, secure and manage that data.
questions.importantPoint: Database = data collection; DBMS = management software.
questions.examTrap: SQL is a language, not the DBMS itself.
questions.hint: Separate the stored information from the software that manages it.

questions.question: In the three-level database architecture, which level describes the overall logical structure of the entire database?

options.text: External level
Conceptual level
Internal level
Physical device level

questions.explanation: The conceptual level describes the overall logical structure of the database, independent of individual user views and physical storage details.
questions.importantPoint: External = user views; conceptual = overall logical structure; internal = storage details.
questions.examTrap: Do not confuse the conceptual schema with an external user view.
questions.hint: Think about the level that sits between user-specific views and physical storage.

questions.question: A bank changes the file organization and adds a new index without changing the logical schema seen by applications. Which type of data independence is demonstrated?

options.text: Logical data independence
Physical data independence
Referential independence
View independence

questions.explanation: Changing storage structures or access paths while preserving the logical schema is physical data independence.
questions.importantPoint: Physical independence concerns changes at the internal/storage level.
questions.examTrap: Changing the conceptual schema while preserving external views is logical data independence.
questions.hint: The change described is below the logical schema.

questions.question: A database has a relation STUDENT(SID, Email, Name), where both SID and Email uniquely identify a student and neither contains unnecessary attributes. Which statement is correct?

options.text: SID and Email are both super keys but neither is a candidate key.
SID and Email are both candidate keys, and one may be chosen as the primary key.
Only SID can be a candidate key because a relation can have only one candidate key.
Email can be a primary key only if SID is removed from the relation.

questions.explanation: Both SID and Email are minimal unique identifiers, so both are candidate keys. One candidate key is selected as the primary key.
questions.importantPoint: A relation can have multiple candidate keys but only one selected primary key.
questions.examTrap: Candidate key means minimal super key; it does not mean the key already selected as primary.
questions.hint: Check uniqueness first, then minimality.

questions.question: For relation R(A,B,C,D), suppose A alone uniquely identifies every tuple. Which of the following is necessarily true?

options.text: A is a candidate key.
A is a super key but cannot be a candidate key.
A must be a foreign key.
A must be a composite key.

questions.explanation: If A uniquely identifies tuples and consists of a single attribute, no proper subset exists, so A is a candidate key.
questions.importantPoint: A minimal unique identifier is a candidate key.
questions.examTrap: A candidate key need not be composite.
questions.hint: Ask whether the unique identifier has any unnecessary attribute.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes a primary key in a relational table?

options.text: It may contain duplicate values as long as a foreign key references it.
It uniquely identifies tuples and does not permit NULL values.
It must always be a single numeric attribute.
It is identical to every candidate key in the relation.

questions.explanation: A primary key is the selected candidate key used to identify tuples; primary-key values must be unique and cannot be NULL.
questions.importantPoint: Primary key = selected candidate key + uniqueness and non-NULL requirement.
questions.examTrap: A composite primary key is valid; it need not be numeric or single-column.
questions.hint: Recall the two core integrity properties of a primary key.

questions.question: Consider EMPLOYEE(EID, Name, DeptID) and DEPARTMENT(DeptID, DeptName). If EMPLOYEE.DeptID references DEPARTMENT.DeptID, which integrity constraint is primarily enforced?

options.text: Entity integrity
Referential integrity
Domain integrity
Key minimality

questions.explanation: The foreign-key reference requires matching referenced values or an allowed NULL, thereby enforcing referential integrity.
questions.importantPoint: Foreign key → referential integrity.
questions.examTrap: Entity integrity is concerned with primary-key uniqueness and non-NULL values.
questions.hint: Look for a relationship between a referencing column and a referenced key.

questions.question: Which operation would directly violate entity integrity for a table whose primary key is STUDENT_ID?

options.text: Inserting a NULL STUDENT_ID
Updating a non-key attribute
Deleting a tuple using its primary key
Inserting a new unique STUDENT_ID

questions.explanation: Entity integrity requires the primary key to be non-NULL. Inserting NULL into the primary key violates that rule.
questions.importantPoint: Entity integrity: primary key values are unique and non-NULL.
questions.examTrap: Referential integrity concerns foreign keys, not the primary key itself.
questions.hint: Focus on what values are forbidden in a primary-key column.

questions.question: A column AGE has a CHECK constraint AGE >= 18. Which operation can be rejected solely because of this constraint?

options.text: INSERT of AGE = 16
INSERT of a unique primary key
SELECT with a WHERE clause
UPDATE of an unrelated column

questions.explanation: The CHECK condition requires AGE to be at least 18, so an inserted value of 16 violates the constraint.
questions.importantPoint: CHECK constraints enforce specified predicates on column values.
questions.examTrap: A CHECK constraint is different from a primary-key uniqueness constraint.
questions.hint: Evaluate the value against AGE >= 18.

questions.question: A relation has three candidate keys: {A}, {B}, and {C,D}. If {B} is selected as the primary key, what remains true about {A}?

options.text: {A} ceases to be a candidate key.
{A} remains a candidate key but is not the primary key.
{A} automatically becomes a foreign key.
{A} must be combined with {B} to remain unique.

questions.explanation: Selecting one candidate key as the primary key does not remove the minimal uniqueness property of the other candidate keys.
questions.importantPoint: Candidate keys are all minimal super keys; primary key is one selected candidate key.
questions.examTrap: Primary-key selection does not change the underlying candidate-key set.
questions.hint: Distinguish “candidate” from “selected as primary.”

questions.question: Which mapping of architecture level to role is correct?

options.text: External → physical storage; Conceptual → user view; Internal → logical schema
External → user-specific view; Conceptual → overall logical schema; Internal → physical storage
External → constraints; Conceptual → indexes; Internal → SQL commands
External → rows; Conceptual → columns; Internal → keys

questions.explanation: The external level provides user-specific views, the conceptual level represents the overall logical schema, and the internal level describes physical storage.
questions.importantPoint: External → view; conceptual → logical structure; internal → storage.
questions.examTrap: Do not map “internal” to internal users; it refers to the storage level.
questions.hint: Read the three levels from user view down to storage.

questions.question: A DBMS allows two applications to use different external views of the same underlying conceptual schema. Which architecture feature enables this?

options.text: Multiple external schemas over a conceptual schema
A separate database for every application
Only physical data independence
Foreign-key cascading

questions.explanation: The external level supports multiple user/application views over the common conceptual schema.
questions.importantPoint: External schemas can provide different views of the same database.
questions.examTrap: Different views do not require duplicate underlying databases.
questions.hint: Think about user-specific views in the three-level architecture.

questions.question: Which of the following is a super key but not a candidate key for relation R(A,B,C) when A alone uniquely identifies tuples?

options.text: {A,B}

questions.explanation: {A,B} is unique because it contains A, but it is not minimal because A alone is already a super key. Therefore {A,B} is a super key but not a candidate key.
questions.importantPoint: Candidate key = minimal super key.
questions.examTrap: Adding attributes to a candidate key usually creates a super key that is no longer minimal.
questions.hint: Check whether a proper subset already identifies the tuple.

questions.question: Suppose a foreign-key column in CHILD references a primary key in PARENT. Which value is generally permitted in CHILD when the relationship is optional?

options.text: Any value, even if it does not occur in PARENT
NULL
A duplicate value only if it is not in PARENT
A value that violates the referenced domain

questions.explanation: When the relationship is optional, the foreign-key column may be NULL unless a NOT NULL constraint is also specified. A non-NULL foreign-key value must satisfy the referential constraint.
questions.importantPoint: Foreign key NULLability depends on whether the relationship is optional and whether NOT NULL is imposed.
questions.examTrap: A foreign key is not required to be unique.
questions.hint: Check whether the relationship is optional before rejecting NULL.

questions.question: Which statement about a UNIQUE constraint is most accurate in standard relational reasoning?

options.text: It identifies the table physically on disk.
It enforces uniqueness for the constrained key/column set, while NULL handling depends on the DBMS and constraint semantics.
It always makes the column the primary key.
It automatically creates a foreign-key relationship.

questions.explanation: A UNIQUE constraint prevents duplicate non-NULL key values under its defined semantics, but it does not make the column the primary key. Exact NULL behavior can vary by DBMS.
questions.importantPoint: UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY are related but not identical constraints.
questions.examTrap: A UNIQUE constraint does not automatically establish referential integrity.
questions.hint: Separate uniqueness from primary-key selection.

questions.question: Which situation is the clearest example of logical data independence?

options.text: Changing an index without changing the logical schema
Changing the conceptual schema while preserving required external views
Changing a disk block size
Reorganizing records within a data file

questions.explanation: Logical data independence concerns changes to the conceptual schema while keeping external views stable as far as possible.
questions.importantPoint: Logical ↔ conceptual structure; physical ↔ storage structures.
questions.examTrap: Index and file-organization changes are physical-level changes.
questions.hint: Identify which architectural level is being modified.

questions.question: A relation R(P,Q,R,S) has candidate key {P,Q}. Which statement about {P,Q,R} is correct?

options.text: It cannot be a super key because it contains a non-key attribute.
It is a super key but not a candidate key.
It is necessarily another candidate key.
It is a foreign key by definition.

questions.explanation: Any superset of a candidate key is a super key because it still uniquely identifies tuples, but {P,Q,R} is not minimal.
questions.importantPoint: Every candidate key is a super key, but not every super key is minimal.
questions.examTrap: A super key may contain extra attributes.
questions.hint: Start with the known candidate key and test whether the larger set is minimal.

questions.question: Which combination is correctly matched?

options.text: Primary key → may be NULL; Foreign key → must always be unique
Candidate key → minimal super key; Super key → uniquely identifies tuples
Super key → must be minimal; Candidate key → may contain redundant attributes
Foreign key → selected candidate key of the same table only

questions.explanation: A candidate key is a minimal super key, while a super key is any attribute set that uniquely identifies tuples and may contain redundant attributes.
questions.importantPoint: Candidate = minimal; super = unique, not necessarily minimal.
questions.examTrap: Do not reverse the definitions of super key and candidate key.
questions.hint: Look for the pair that preserves the word “minimal.”

questions.question: A DBMS changes the internal storage structure while applications continue to use the same conceptual schema and external views. Which statement best describes the benefit?

options.text: Applications need not be rewritten merely because physical storage changed.
Every external view must be redesigned.
All candidate keys must change.
The database must be converted to a different model.

questions.explanation: Physical data independence allows internal storage changes without requiring corresponding changes to higher-level schemas or applications.
questions.importantPoint: Higher levels are insulated from many internal storage changes.
questions.examTrap: Physical changes do not imply a change in the data model.
questions.hint: Focus on the phrase “internal storage structure.”

questions.question: A table has PRIMARY KEY(A,B) and a separate UNIQUE(C). Which statement is necessarily correct?

options.text: C is the primary key.
{A,B} is the selected primary key, while C has a uniqueness constraint.
A and B must each be unique individually.
C must be a foreign key.

questions.explanation: PRIMARY KEY(A,B) defines a composite primary key. UNIQUE(C) separately enforces uniqueness on C according to the DBMS semantics.
questions.importantPoint: A composite primary key can consist of multiple attributes.
questions.examTrap: A composite primary key does not imply A and B are individually unique.
questions.hint: Read the constraint declarations independently.
